abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: SIRT2, the cytoplasmic member of the sirtuin family, is generally acknowledged to promote cancer and contribute to the progression of various pathologies, including neurodegeneration, inflammation, obesity, and bacterial infection through the deacetylation of target substrates. In our previous efforts we identified potent and highly selective SIRT2 inhibitors with IC50 values in the micromolar range. To further optimize their activity, we performed molecular docking‐guided design and subsequent synthesis of a series of novel 1,3,4‐thiadiazole derivatives. SIRT inhibitory screening identified that ST131 and ST132 achieved moderate inhibitory effects against SIRT2 with IC50 values of 8.95 and 6.62 µM, respectively. Moreover, cellular assays in MCF‐7 breast cancer cells revealed that ST132 has shown an antiproliferative effect, as well as increased acetylated α‐tubulin expression levels, which is typically consistent with SIRT2 inhibition. In addition, docking studies were performed to analyze and rationalize the structural differences responsible for SIRT2 activity, shedding light on the importance of the interactions occurring at the entrance of the binding site. Finally, molecular mechanics‐generalized born surface area (MM‐GBSA) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation approaches were conducted to verify the stability of ST132 in the complex with SIRT2.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Sirtuins (SIRTs), consisting of seven members (SIRT1‐7) belonging to the class III histone deacetylase (HDAC) enzyme family, have retained their structure throughout eukaryotic evolution. All SIRTs share a highly conserved central NAD⁺‐binding site and catalytic core domain (Mei et al. 2016). However, variations in their N‐ and C‐terminal extensions result in distinct subcellular distributions: SIRT1, SIRT6, and SIRT7 are predominantly localized within the nucleus though a fraction of SIRT1 is also found in cytosol; SIRT3‐5 are mitochondrial; and SIRT2 shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm during cell division but resides mainly in the cytoplasm (Roshdy et al. 2021). This diversity influences their biological functions, substrate specificity, interactions with cellular binding partners, and enzymatic activity (Chen et al. 2021).

In the nucleus, SIRT2 has been reported to deacetylate histones H3K18, H3K56, and H4K16 (Shen et al. 2024; Jing and Lin 2015), while in the cytoplasm it targets several nonhistone substrates, including α‐tubulin, FOXO3a, p65, p300, p53, HIF‐1α, NF‐κB, and PGC‐1α. These substrates are associated with cell cycle, transcriptional regulation, microtubule dynamics, cell death, metabolism, stress responses, and inflammation (Wang et al. 2007; Black et al. 2008; Rothgiesser et al. 2010; Peck et al. 2010). Therefore, dysregulation of SIRT2 has been linked to various diseases, such as neurodegenerative disorders, cancer, tissue fibrosis (e.g., lung, kidney, liver), cardiac injury, metabolic disorders, viral and bacterial infections (Mei et al. 2016; Zhu et al. 2022; Zhang et al. 2020; Kaya and Eren 2023; Duran‐Castells et al. 2023; Eskandarian et al. 2013; Akbulut 2025; Shenk et al. 2024).

Several studies have demonstrated that SIRT2 acts both as a tumor suppressor and a promoter depending on tissue type, cancer stage, and specific cellular context, owing to its involvement in multiple cellular pathways (Shen et al. 2024; Kaya and Eren 2023; Kim et al. 2011). Additionally, evidence indicates that depletion or inhibition of SIRT2 can lead to anticancer effects, underscoring its potential as a therapeutic target (Dan et al. 2012; Liu et al. 2013; Chen et al. 2013; Hou et al. 2012; McGlynn et al. 2014; Fiorentino et al. 2024). Nevertheless, its dual role in cancer introduces significant complexity and unlocking the therapeutic promise of SIRT2 requires the development of potent inhibitors. Furthermore, recent studies reported that high doses of pan‐SIRT1‐3 inhibitors cause severe toxicity compared to selective SIRT2 inhibitors, despite exhibiting similar cytotoxicity toward cancer cells, emphasizing the critical importance of SIRT2 selectivity in anticancer drug design (Hong et al. 2021).

Several SIRT2 inhibitors with diverse chemotypes have been identified (Kaya and Eren 2023; Fiorentino et al. 2024; Xue et al. 2023; Bursch et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2020), which can be clustered them into four main groups according to their binding modes and inhibition kinetics: (i) mechanism‐based inhibitors, (ii) substrate‐mimicking inhibitors, (iii) C‐pocket binders, and (iv) selectivity pocket‐binding inhibitors (Bernhard et al. 2025). However, no SIRT2 inhibitor has yet been approved for clinical use, likely due to challenges such as insufficient inhibitory potency, low selectivity, limited bioavailability, and poor pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic characteristics (Kaya and Eren 2023; Fiorentino et al. 2024). Therefore, further in‐depth investigations are essential to fully elucidate the therapeutic potential of SIRT2 inhibitors.

The general structural characteristics of SIRT2 comprise a leucine‐rich nuclear export signal (NES) motif within the N‐terminal region, a large domain featuring a Rossmann fold, which surrounds the NAD+‐binding site, and a small domain consisting of structural zinc‐binding module (Finnin et al. 2001). These two domains are connected by four or five crossover loops, forming a prominent cleft that constitutes the enzyme active site. Within this cleft, NAD+ and the acetyl‐lysine substrate enter from opposite sides to bind. Substrate binding induces the formation of a conserved, predominantly hydrophobic tunnel that accommodates the acetyl‐lysine side chain, thereby facilitating catalysis. Additionally, a specific pocket within the active site, lined with hydrophobic residues and intersecting the groove between the two domains, is thought to serve as a class‐specific binding site that enables SIRT2 to selectively recognize its substrates (Figure 1).

(B) Close‐up view of the SIRT2 active site highlighting key residues forming the substrate‐binding channel, ECS, and selectivity pocket (PDB: 5DY4). (C) Structural comparison of the SIRT2 active site illustrating additional residues at the entrance of the substrate‐binding channel (PDB: 5YQO).

sec.p: In recent years, several X‐ray crystal structures of SIRT2 have been elucidated, either in the apo form or complexed with substrates and various class‐specific inhibitors (Colcerasa et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2018; Roche et al. 2023; Rumpf et al. 2015). These structural studies have provided crucial insights into the catalytic roles of key residues and the molecular architecture of the SIRT2 active site (Bernhard et al. 2025). Based on these findings, the SIRT2 active site can be divided into four distinct structural regions: the substrate‐binding tunnel, the NAD+‐binding region (comprising the A‐, B‐, and C‐pockets), the extended C‐site (ECS), and the selectivity pocket. Selective SIRT2 inhibitors typically occupy both the substrate‐binding site and the ECS, interacting with several hydrophobic residues such as Y104, F119, F131, F234, F235, L134, L138, P140, I169, I232, and V233 through hydrophobic contacts, H‐bonds, and π–π stacking interactions mediated by their alkyl or aromatic moieties. Importantly, these inhibitors can also induce the formation of a selectivity pocket defined by residues I93, A135, L138, P140, F143, L206, and I213. Within this pocket, they engage in π‐π stacking interactions with Y139 and F190, adopting a rigid conformation that fits precisely within the SIRT2 active site. Additional polar contacts with R97 and V233 and π‐π stacking with F235 further enhance inhibitory potency. Moreover, a water‐mediated H‐bond with P94 in the cofactor‐binding loop has been shown to stabilize the active‐site conformation, contributing to increased inhibitor affinity. Finally, interaction with residue E237 has been proposed as a key determinant for the development of next‐generation SIRT2 inhibitors with improved potency and cellular efficacy (Vogelmann et al. 2022; Schiedel et al. 2016; Yang et al. 2017; Sinatra et al. 2023; Friedrich et al. 2025) (Figure 1).

During our efforts to develop novel SIRT2 inhibitors, we have established a comprehensive in‐house compound library comprising N‐aryl(aryloxy)acetamide, aryloxybenzamide, 1,3,4‐oxadiazole/thiadiazole‐2‐arylthioacetamide, benzyl(1,3,4‐thiadiazole)carboxamide, and 2,7‐disubstituted 9H‐fluoren‐9‐one scaffolds, all of which have been identified as SIRT2 inhibitory frameworks (Eren et al. 2019; Yagci et al. 2021; Gozelle et al. 2022, 2024; Kaya, Eren, Massarotti, et al. 2024; Kaya, Eren, Massarotti, Gunindi, et al. 2024; Gozelle et al. 2025; Aksel et al. 2025). According to gained structure‐activity relationship (SAR) data, the initial diphenyl compound ST59 (Gozelle et al. 2024) containing a methylene linker, exhibited weak SIRT2 inhibition (42% at 100 µM). Replacement of the central phenyl ring with a 1,3,4‐thiadiazole core, as in ST109 and ST113 (Aksel et al. 2025), resulted in a slight enhancement in inhibitory potency (46% and 49% at 100 µM, respectively), confirming the importance of the geometric orientation imposed by the central ring located within the ECS. In contrast, substitution of the methylene linker with an oxygen atom in ST61 (Kaya, Eren, Massarotti, et al. 2024) caused a complete loss of activity, likely due to disruption of the optimal orientation and hydrophobic interactions. Interestingly, ST49 (Gozelle et al. 2024), bearing an oxygen linker and a methylated nitrogen atom instead of sulfur as the phenyl‐to‐acetamide linker, showed remarkable improvement in activity (50% at 100 µM).

Overall, this brief analysis guided us to preserve the 1,3,4‐thiadiazole core, together with the (methylamino)acetamide connector at its second position as a structural framework, since the nature of the heterocyclic core and linker atoms critically determines SIRT2 selectivity and inhibitory potency.

To achieve additional interactions at the entrance of the substrate‐binding site, the thiadiazole ring was substituted at the fifth position with various alkyl‐aryl groups (Figure 2). Accordingly, the designed compounds (ST118‐ST141) feature a 1,3,4‐thiadiazole ring with a 2‐[(2/3‐fluoro‐ or 3‐methylphenyl)methylamino]acetamide fragment at position 2 and diverse phenyl‐based substituents at position 5, attached via oxymethylene or ethyl linkers. These substituents, presented as region A, including 4‐acetamido, 4‐[2‐(3‐cyanophenyl)acetamido], 4‐(isoxazole‐5‐carboxamido), 4‐(3‐dimethylamino)propanamido, and 4‐(benzo[d] (Mei et al. 2016; Chen et al. 2021) dioxol‐5‐carboxamido)phenyl groups were chosen to ensure structural diversity and to enable π–π stacking as well as hydrogen bonding interactions at the substrate‐binding tunnel entrance. Similarly, the substituents and their positions on the phenyl ring in region B were determined based on previously obtained data and molecular docking results, which demonstrated their role in promoting the appropriate binding conformation and orientation within the SIRT2 active site.

sec.title: Synthesis
sec.p: As illustrated in Scheme 1, the synthesis of the target compounds ST118‐ST141 began with the preparation of N‐methyl‐N‐phenylglycine derivatives (1a–1c), which were obtained via the substitution reaction of the corresponding N‐methylanilines with methyl 2‐bromoacetate, followed by ester hydrolysis. In parallel, heating 3‐(4‐nitrophenyl)propanoic acid or 2‐(4‐nitrophenoxy)acetic acid with thiosemicarbazide in the presence of POCl3 afforded the corresponding 2‐amino‐1,3,4‐thiadiazoles (2a and 2b). Then, amide coupling of compounds 1a–1c with 2a or 2b in the presence of EDC and DMAP yielded all target amide derivatives (3a, 3b, 3d–3f) except 3c. In the case of 3c, compound 2a was first reacted with bromoacetyl bromide, followed by the substitution reaction of the resulting intermediate with N,3‐dimethylaniline. Subsequently, reduction of the nitro group in compounds 3a–3f afforded the corresponding amine derivatives (4a–4f). In the final step, acetylation of the aminophenyl moiety of 4a–4f yielded the target compounds ST118‐ST123, whereas amide coupling of 4a–4f with the corresponding carboxylic acids in the presence of EDC and DMAP afforded compounds ST124‐ST141. The structures of the compounds were confirmed by 1H‐NMR, 13C‐NMR, and HRMS spectra, which were presented in Supporting Information.

sec.title: Biological Evaluation
sec.p: The synthesized compounds were evaluated for their SIRT2 inhibitory potency with the standard fluorescent‐based assay. Among the synthesized compounds, those exhibiting more than 50% inhibition of SIRT2 activity were tested also for their inhibitory activity towards the SIRT1 and SIRT3 enzymes. The results are summarized in Table 1.

fn.p: Abbreviations: n.d., not determined; n.i., no inhibition (< 5% inhibition); SD, standard deviation (n = 3).

sec.p: The compounds evaluated in this study generally exhibited SIRT2 inhibition at 50 µM inhibitor concentration, suggesting that the compound scaffold may be compatible with SIRT2. According to the findings obtained, modification of the X linker influenced SIRT2 inhibitory potency. Compounds incorporating a methylene (CH2) linker displayed the highest inhibitory activity compared to those bearing an oxygen atom as the linker. These results imply that a certain degree of flexibility within the linker region is beneficial for optimal positioning within the active site. Substitution on the terminal phenyl ring, oriented towards selectivity pocket, also significantly affected activity. In particular, 3‐substituted derivatives (3‐F and 3‐CH3; ST131: 58% and ST132: 54%) consistently exhibited superior SIRT2 inhibition relative to 2‐F analogs (ST130: 39%). With respect to the A region, notable differences in SIRT2 inhibition were observed depending on the aromatic system employed. Among the series, compounds containing methyl group showed diminished activity, whereas replacement of the methyl group with benzyl or oxygen‐containing heterocyclic rings enhanced SIRT2 inhibition. This suggests that the electron‐rich aromatic system contribute positively to binding, favoring hydrophobic and π‐π stacking interactions within the substrate‐binding tunnel entrance, comprising the residues F119, F131, H187, F234, V233, F235, E237. The compounds containing an isoxazole moiety exhibited the highest activity, particularly when the X linker was a methylene group (ST131 and ST132). For the compounds featuring bulkier rings in the A region, it was noticed that although the 1,3‐benzodioxole analog (ST140: 85%) displayed the highest individual SIRT2 inhibition, the overall inhibitory potency of these bulkier A ring derivatives was generally lower than that of the isoxazole‐based analogs. These findings indicate that the isoxazole moiety offers an optimal steric fit for the entrance of the substrate‐binding channel. Taken together, these findings highlight that a flexible methylene linker combined with meta‐oriented substituents on the terminal phenyl ring and isoxazole ring in the A region provides the most favorable structural features for SIRT2 inhibition within this series, highlighting the importance of both linker flexibility and steric optimization for achieving high potency.

For the compounds exhibiting more than 50% inhibition of SIRT2 (ST125, ST131, ST132, ST135, and ST140), IC50 values were calculated by nonlinear sigmoidal dose‐response fitting of the complete data using GraphPad Prism 10 (Table S1, Figure S1). To evaluate selectivity, SIRT1 and SIRT3 activities were also assessed at 50 µM inhibitor concentration. The corresponding data are presented in Table 1. Based on the calculated IC50 values, ST131 and ST132 were distinguished by their potent SIRT2 inhibition in the low micromolar range (8.95 and 6.62 µM, respectively) among the compounds. No significant inhibition was observed against SIRT1 for any of the tested compounds, whereas all analogs except ST132 (11%) exhibited inhibition of SIRT3 enzymatic activity ranging from 31% to 68%. Accordingly, ST132 was identified as the most potent and selective SIRT2 inhibitor within the series.

Given that pharmacological evidence obtained using several structurally distinct selective SIRT2 inhibitors strongly suggests that SIRT2 is a promising target for breast cancer therapy (Shah et al. 2016), the antiproliferative effects of the SIRT2‐inhibitory compounds ST125, ST131, ST132, ST135, and ST140 were evaluated on the human MCF‐7 breast cancer cell line using the MTT assay. All tested compounds exhibited dose‐dependent cytotoxic activity with varying potency. ST125 reduced cell viability in a dose‐dependent manner, with an IC50 value of 51.89 µM, and statistically significant effects were observed at concentrations ≥ 25 µM (p < 0.0001). ST131 demonstrated comparable potency (IC50 = 49.26 µM) and produced detectable growth inhibition from 25 µM upward. ST132, identified as the only selective SIRT2 inhibitor, also displayed measurable antiproliferative activity with an IC50 value of 72.41 µM, showing significant reductions in cell viability at ≥ 50 µM (p < 0.0001). ST135 exhibited a similar concentration‐dependent response (IC50 = 71.97 µM), predominantly at higher concentrations, while ST140 was the least potent compound with an IC50 value of 84.30 µM, with statistically significant effects only at 100 and 200 µM (Figure 3).

caption.p: Cell viability (%) of MCF‐7 cells after 72 h treatment with various concentrations of the tested compounds. Data are expressed as mean ± SD (n = 3). Statistical significance compared with the untreated control is indicated as *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, and ****p < 0.0001.

sec.p: Although ST132 did not display the strongest antiproliferative effect among the tested compounds, it was selected for Western blot analysis because of its superior SIRT2 selectivity. Accordingly, to examine whether ST132 modulates protein acetylation in MCF‐7 cells, Western blot was performed on cell lysates to examine changes in the acetylation level of α‐tubulin, a well‐known substrate of SIRT2. Based on the results, ST132 was found to have a notable impact on SIRT2‐mediated deacetylation of α‐tubulin, resulting in substrate hyperacetylation. Western blot analysis also revealed a significant decrease in SIRT2 protein levels upon ST132 treatment, indicating that the enhanced α‐tubulin acetylation may be due not only to direct enzymatic inhibition but also to reduced SIRT2 expression. Moreover, the observed antiproliferative effect of ST132 (IC50 = 72.41 µM) in MCF‐7 cells is consistent with its SIRT2 inhibition, suggesting that its cytotoxicity may be associated with SIRT2‐dependent mechanisms (Figure 4).

caption.p: Western blots showing relative protein expression levels of SIRT2, α‐tubulin, acetylated α‐tubulin with that of β‐actin. Significant differences are indicated as *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01.

sec.title: Molecular Modeling
sec.p: To gain insight into the correlation between the observed inhibitory activity and the binding patterns of the inhibitors identified herein (ST125, ST131, ST132, ST135, and ST140) within the active sites of SIRT2 and SIRT3, molecular docking simulations were conducted, and the predicted binding poses were analyzed in comparison with those of the corresponding co‐crystallized ligands.

According to the docked SIRT2‐inhibitor complexes obtained, in ST132, the best performing compound, the terminal 3‐methylphenyl moiety was oriented toward the selectivity pocket, while the distal isoxazole ring was positioned toward the substrate‐binding tunnel entrance. Within the selectivity pocket, the compound formed the desired interactions, including π‐π stackings with Y139 and F190, and a water‐mediated H‐bond with P94 in the ECS region. Additionally, π‐π contacts between the central 1,3,4‐thiadiazole ring and F96 were observed in this region. On the other hand, in the substrate‐binding channel, where our design strategy aimed to introduce additional interactions, the phenyl ring located between the isoxazole‐thiadiazole moieties engaged in π‐π interactions with F119 and F234. The amide carbonyl attached to this phenyl ring formed H‐bonds with both R97 and H187. Lastly, the distal isoxazole established a π–π stacking contact with H187, effectively anchoring the compound within the targeted region (Figure 5).

caption.p: Proposed binding mode for ST132 within the SIRT2 active site (PDB: 8OWZ) depicted by the surface mesh with a binding energy of −11.94 kcal/mol. H‐bonds and π–π contacts are represented by yellow and cyan dashed lines, respectively.

sec.p: Except for ST135, the compounds exhibited SIRT2 inhibitory potency (ST125, ST131, and ST140) shared a common accommodation within the SIRT2 active site. Their terminal 3‐fluoro/methylphenyl rings interacted with residues in the selectivity pocket, while their 1,3,4‐thiadiazole cores engaged with F96 in the ECS region. In addition, all three compounds formed π‐π stacking contacts with F119 and F234 at the entrance of the substrate‐binding tunnel. Water‐mediated H‐bonds with P94 in the ECS were observed only for ST131 and ST140. The main difference detected in the binding modes of all four compounds (ST125, ST131, ST132, and ST140) was due to the interactions formed at the entrance of the substrate‐binding site by the structural extensions we incorporated into our earlier compounds. The interactions formed by the introduced distal rings (3‐cyanophenyl: ST125; isoxazole: ST131, ST132, ST135; benzo[d] (Mei et al. 2016; Chen et al. 2021) dioxol: ST140)—particularly the isoxazole ring, which was identified as the most favorable according to the docking results‐ were consistent with the biological data. The binding strength of these rings contributed to stabilizing the active conformation, and this stabilization correlated well with the experimental findings. In contrast, ST135 adopted a markedly different orientation within the active site. Instead of extending toward the selectivity pocket, it bent into a U‐shaped conformation and positioned itself between the substrate‐binding tunnel and the NAD+‐binding region. With this conformation, ST135 formed a H‐bond between its acetamide nitrogen and V233, while its 1,3,4‐thiadiazole core engaged in π‐cation and π–π interactions with R97 and H187, respectively. In addition, the distal isoxazole ring established π–π interactions with Y104 (Figure 6).

caption.p: Predicted binding poses of ST125 (A), ST131 (B), ST135 (C), ST140 (D) within the SIRT2 active site (PDB: 8OWZ) with binding energies of −11.84, −11.80, −9.77, and −11.73 kcal/mol, respectively. H‐bonds, π–π contacts, and π‐cation interactions are represented by yellow, cyan, and green dashed lines, respectively.

sec.p: Compounds ST135 and ST140, which, in addition to SIRT2, also displayed substantial inhibitory activity against SIRT3 (67% and 68% inhibition @50 µM, respectively), were docked into the SIRT3 active site (PDB: 4JSR) and the resulting poses were analyzed in comparison with the co‐crystallized ligand. The inhibitor 1NQ formed π–π interactions between its thieno[3,2‐d]pyrimidine ring and F157, as well as a H‐bond between the pyrimidine nitrogen (N1) and the F157 backbone. The carbonyl of the 6‐carboxamide group accepted H‐bonds from I230 and D231, while the 6‐carboxamide nitrogen engaged in H‐bonding with A146, I154, and D231. Lastly, along the substrate‐binding channel, the aryl amide NH interacted with V292 through H‐bonding and the distal ethylamide substituted on the 2‐thiophene formed H‐bonds with E296 and E325 (Figure 7A) (Disch et al. 2013). The docked compounds ST135 and ST140 were positioned in the SIRT3 active site in a manner similar to the coligand. Accordingly, the NH group of the acetamide moieties attached to 1,3,4‐thiadiazole ring formed H‐bonds with E296 and E325 through their carbonyl groups. The phenyl rings connected to the linker engaged in π‐π stacking contacts with H248. Additionally, both ST135 and ST140 established a H‐bond with I230 via their corresponding distal rings. Overall, the molecular docking results suggested that the key H‐bonding interactions identified within the active site account for the SIRT3 inhibitory activities of both compounds, whereas their comparatively fewer interactions relative to the coligand explain the differences in the level of SIRT3 inhibition observed (Figure 7).

caption.p: The bioactive conformation of 1NQ (A) and proposed binding modes for ST135 (B) and ST140 (C) within the SIRT3 active site (PDB: 4JSR) with binding energies of −6.09 and −8.37 kcal/mol, respectively. H‐bonds and π–π contacts are represented by yellow and cyan dashed lines, respectively.

sec.p: Using the MM‐GBSA approach, we estimated the binding free energy of the SIRT2‐ST132 complex, obtaining a favorable ΔG_bind value of −101.07 kcal/mol, supporting a high affinity of ST132 for the binding site (Table 2).

caption.p: MM‐GBSA energies (kcal/mol) for docking pose of ST132 binding at the SIRT2 active site.

sec.p: To further evaluate the dynamic stability of the docked pose, ST132 was subjected to an explicit‐solvent MD simulation. Briefly, the SIRT2‐ST132 complex was immersed in an orthorhombic simulation box filled with TIP4P water molecules, and the solvated system was neutralized and equilibrated according to the workflow adopted in our previous studies. The production run was then carried out for 500 ns under NPT conditions (300 K, 1 bar) using the Desmond implemented in Schrödinger Small‐Molecule Drug Discovery Suite.

To monitor the impact of the simulation on complex stability, RMSD values were computed along the trajectory. The protein backbone (Cα atoms) remained stable from the early stages of the simulation, showing RMSD fluctuations within ~2.0–3.5 Å (Figure S3), consistent with a well‐equilibrated system. RMSF analysis highlighted localized flexibility, with the most evident fluctuations mapped to the 240–250 region (Figure S4), in agreement with previously observed behavior for SIRT2 systems. Notably, ST132 rapidly converged to a stable binding mode within the pocket, with the ligand/complex RMSD stabilizing around ~6 Å relative to the initial pose, without signs of progressive drift or pocket escape across the 500 ns trajectory (Figure S5).

Trajectory inspection confirmed the persistence of key hydrophobic/aromatic contacts throughout the simulation (Figure S6). In particular, interactions involving F119 at the substrate‐binding tunnel entrance and F190 within the selectivity pocket were maintained for the entire simulation time, coherently supporting the binding mode proposed by docking and reinforcing the role of these residues in anchoring ST132 in the SIRT2 active site.

sec.title: Chemistry
sec.p: All the chemicals were purchased from commercial suppliers (Abcr, Acros Organics, BLDpharm, Sigma‐Aldrich) and used without further purification. TLC for reaction monitoring was employed using alumina plates coated with Merck silica gel 60 F254, visualized under UV light at 254 or 366 nm. 1H‐NMR and 13C‐NMR spectra were recorded using a Varian Mercury 400 MHz high‐performance digital FT‐NMR spectrometer and a Bruker Avance NEO 500 MHz FT‐NMR spectrometer, with tetramethylsilane (TMS) as the internal standard. Chemical shifts were reported in δ (ppm) relative to TMS, with DMSO‐d 6 as the solvent, and all coupling constants were expressed in Hertz (Hz). HRMS data were acquired using a Waters LCT Premier XE UPLC/MS‐TOF system with positive (ESI⁺) electrospray ionization mode. For chromatographic separation, an ACQUITY BEH C18 column (2.1 × 50 mm, 1.7 µm, Waters Corporation) was employed as the stationary phase, using a gradient mobile phase of water and acetonitrile (80:20 → 10:90) at a flow rate of 0.25 ml/min. Melting points were determined without correction by the Stuart SMP50 automatic melting point apparatus.

sec.title: General Procedure for the Preparation of 1a–1c
sec.p: A mixture of appropriate N‐methylaniline derivative (1 equiv.) and methyl 2‐bromoacetate (1.2 equiv.) were refluxed in methanol in the presence of sodium acetate (2 equiv.) for periods ranging from 24 to 48 h. After completion of the reaction, the mixture was cooled and concentrated under reduced pressure. The residue was diluted with ethyl acetate and extracted with a 1% aqueous NaHCO3 solution (3 × 10 mL), followed by brine (3 × 10 mL). The combined organic layers were dried over anhydrous Na2SO4 and concentrated in vacuo. The obtained crude methyl N‐methyl‐N‐phenylglycinate derivative (1 equiv.) was heated in a 10% aqueous NaOH solution at 50°C overnight. Upon completion, the reaction mixture was cooled, acidified to pH 3 with concentrated HCl, and extracted with ethyl acetate (3 × 10 mL), followed by brine (3 × 10 mL). The combined organic layers were dried over anhydrous Na2SO4 and concentrated under reduced pressure. The resulting crude product was used directly in the subsequent step without further purification.

sec.title: General Procedure for the Preparation of 2a and 2b
sec.p: The appropriate carboxylic acid derivative (1 equiv.) and thiosemicarbazide (1.1 equiv.) were heated in POCl3 at 80°C for 1 h. After cooling, water was added to the reaction mixture, which was then heated again at 80°C for an additional 4–6 h. sec.title: SIRT1‐3 Inhibition Assay
sec.p: The inhibitory activities of the synthesized compounds against SIRT1, SIRT2, and SIRT3 enzymes were evaluated using a SIRT2 Screening Assay Kit (Abcam, ab133082) and Direct Fluorescent Screening Assay Kits for SIRT1 and SIRT3 (Cayman, 10010401 and 10011566) according to the manufacturers' instructions (Kaya, Eren, Massarotti, Gunindi, et al. 2024). The synthesized compounds, along with suramin and EX‐527 as reference inhibitors were tested at a screening concentration of 50 μM. To exclude compound‐related optical artefacts, intrinsic autofluorescence and potential compound‐fluorophore interference were evaluated prior to enzymatic measurements under assay‐mimicking conditions in the absence of enzyme, following the manufacturer's instructions. No compound‐derived fluorescence or optical interference at levels influencing enzymatic activity measurements was observed. In brief, the assay mixture contained test compounds dissolved in DMSO (5 µL/well; final DMSO ≤ 1%), SIRT assay buffer (25 µl/well), human recombinant SIRT1/2/3 enzymes (5 µL/well), and substrate solution (15 µL/well). Plates were incubated at 37°C for 45 min with shaking, after which developer solution (50 µL/well) was added to terminate the reaction, followed by an additional incubation at room temperature for 30 min. The resulting fluorescence was recorded at excitation/emission wavelengths of 360/460 nm using a Molecular Devices SpectraMax i3x microplate reader. Each experiment was performed in triplicate. Fluorescence values were normalized to those of the blank wells, and percent inhibition was calculated for each compound. Compounds displaying > 50% inhibition toward SIRT2 were further subjected to dose‐response analysis for IC50 determination using GraphPad Prism 10, with concentrations ranging from 0.1 to 300 µM.

sec.title: Antiproliferative Assay
sec.p: The antiproliferative activities of the selected compounds against the human MCF‐7 breast cancer cell line were evaluated using the MTT assay (Kuźma et al. 2012; Mosmann 1983). MCF‐7 cells (5 × 104 cells/mL) were seeded into 96‐well plates and treated with the compounds at concentrations ranging from 1 to 200 μM, followed by the incubation at 37°C in a 5% CO2 atmosphere. Untreated cells were used as the control group. After 72 h of incubation, MTT reagent (5 mg/mL) was added to each well, and the plates were incubated for an additional 4 h. Subsequently, the medium was carefully aspirated, and the resulting formazan crystals were dissolved. Absorbance in each well was measured at 540 nm using a Molecular Devices SpectraMax i3x microplate reader. The experiment was performed four times for each test compound. IC50 values were calculated from dose‐response analysis plotting percent cell viability versus compound concentration using GraphPad Prism 10. Data obtained from cell culture experiments were expressed as mean ± SD, and one‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used for multiple comparisons.

sec.title: Western Blot Analysis
sec.p: MCF‐7 cells (2.5 × 106 cells/mL) were seeded in 6‐well plates and treated with the test compound in selected concentration according to the MTT assay, followed by the incubation at 37°C in a 5% CO2 atmosphere. After 72 h of incubation, the cells were detached using trypsin and centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 5 min. The resulting cell pellets were washed once with 1xPBS buffer and centrifuged again under the same conditions, followed by incubation in cell lysis buffer at 0°C for 30 min. After incubation, the lysates were centrifuged at 14.000g for 10 min at 4°C, and the supernatants were transferred to separate microtubes. The obtained lysates were applied on SDS‐PAGE gel containing 25 μg protein and subjected to electrophoresis for 1 h. Proteins were then transferred to the nitrocellulose membranes using a semi‐dry transfer device and washed three times with 1xPBS buffer. Membranes were blocked with 5% skimmed milk powder in PBS for 1.5 h, followed by incubation with primary antibodies overnight at 4°C. After washing three times with PBS‐Tween solution, membranes were incubated with secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Finally, membranes were washed three times with PBS‐Tween solution and visualized using a Li‐Cor Odyssey FC imaging system (Bakar‐Ates et al. 2020).

sec.title: Molecular Docking
sec.p: The molecular docking studies were performed using the Glide module implemented in the Schrödinger Small‐Molecule Drug Discovery Suite (Small‐Molecule Drug Discovery Suite 2024‐4, Schrödinger LLC, New York, NY, 2024). The hSIRT2 (PDB: 8OWZ) (Sinatra et al. 2023) and hSIRT3 (PDB: 4JSR) (Disch et al. 2013) X‐ray crystal structures were retrieved from the RCSB Protein Data Bank and further prepared at physiological pH using the Protein Preparation Wizard tool. During the preparation stage, atom types and charges were assigned, missing hydrogen atoms were added, and all water molecules (except HOH573 and HOH676 for 8OWZ; HOH531 and HOH632 for 4JSR) were removed. Finally, energy minimization and refinement were done up to RMSD cutoff of 0.20 Å (for 8OWZ) and 0.30 Å (for 4JSR) by applying an OPLS4 force field. Each grid box, containing the active site coordinates of the proteins, was defined with a 20 Å radius around the coligand using Receptor Grid Generation tool, applying default parameters and OPLS4 force field. The docking protocols for both proteins were validated by redocking the corresponding coligand and calculating RMSD values between their docked and bioactive conformations, which were 0.3733 Å for SIRT2 and 0.1233 Å for SIRT3, demonstrating the accuracy of pose predictions. The 3D structures of all compounds were prepared using the LigPrep module and docked into hSIRT2 and hSIRT3 using the XP mode of Glide, with a van der Waals (vdW) radius scaling factor of 0.80 and partial charge cutoffs of 0.12 and 0.15, respectively. The resulting docking poses were subsequently rescored using Prime MM‐GBSA to estimate ligand binding energies, and the best pose for each compound was selected based on the docking score and favorable binding interactions.

sec.title: MD Simulations
sec.p: MD simulations were carried out to investigate the stability and dynamic behavior of the SIRT2‐ST132 docked complex, following a protocol consistent with previously reported studies (Kaya, Eren, Massarotti, et al. 2024; Mellini et al. 2017) was used to analyze the selected docked complexes using the Desmond module. The simulation system was constructed under physiological conditions employing an explicit solvent model with the TIP4P water model in an orthorhombic box (10 × 10 × 10 Å), supplemented with 0.15 M salt. To ensure overall electrical neutrality, counter ions, specifically Na+ and Cl−, were placed at a minimum distance of 20 Å from the ligand within the simulation system. Subsequently, system relaxation was conducted in multiple stages. Initially, energy minimization was performed for up to 2000 minimization steps using a force constant of 50 kcal/mol/Å2, with harmonic restraints applied to the solute atoms. This was followed by a 12 ps MD simulation at 10 K with a force constant of 50 kcal/mol/Å2 under the NPT ensemble using Berendsen thermostat and barostat, while maintaining the same restraints. Subsequently, the system was heated from 10 to 300 K over a 24 ps period under NPT conditions with harmonic restraints. A further 24 ps equilibration was carried out at 300 K without harmonic restraints using the Nose‐Hoover thermostat and Martyna‐Tobias‐Klein barostat. Following relaxation of the system, the docked complex underwent a 500 ns MD simulation using default parameters under the NPT ensemble. The resulting trajectories were meticulously analyzed to evaluate structural stability and interaction patterns through calculations of RMSD, RMSF, and protein‐ligand interaction profiles using simulation interaction diagrams.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Herein, we designed new 1,3,4‐thiadiazole‐based SIRT2 inhibitors by incorporating the structural requirements previously identified from our earlier SIRT2 inhibitors. In particular, the molecular scaffolds were extended to enable additional interactions at the entrance of substrate‐binding channel. With this strategy, we aimed to enhance binding affinity toward SIRT2 and provide guidance for structure‐based drug design in future studies. Biological evaluations allowed the identification of ST132 as the most promising selective SIRT2 inhibitor, with an IC50 value of 6.62 µM. ST132, which has been validated for its inhibitory potential against SIRT2 by Western blot analysis, exhibited a moderate antiproliferative effect in MCF‐7 cells (IC50 = 72.41 µM), suggesting a close relationship between SIRT2‐dependent mechanisms and its effects on cell viability. In silico studies supported this design rationale, indicating that the newly designed molecules establish more extensive interactions with the SIRT2 active site and may therefore exhibit enhanced inhibitory potency. Overall, these findings confirm the validity of our structure‐based optimization approach and pave the way for further improvements in the field of SIRT2 inhibitors in future work.
